newsitem.title: UK: British stocks at new record after rate rise.
newsitem.headline: British stocks at new record after rate rise.

text.p: British shares surged to a new record high on Thursday as financial markets reacted positively to another rise in Bank of England interest rates.

The latest increase was seen as the last monetary tightening in the current cycle and government bond prices also rose. The pound sterling eased, no longer supported by prospects of yet higher interest rates.
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee said it was raising official interest rates by 1/4 point to seven percent.

It was the fourth rise in as many months but in a statement the committee hinted strongly that rates may well now have peaked, good news for British exporters whose profits have been hit by a soaring pound.
"Upward pressures on the exchange rate should be reduced by the perception that interest rates have reached a level consistent with the inflation target," the committee said.
It was that line which convinced markets that the Bank of England now thought it had done enough to keep underlying inflation on course to meet the government target of 2.5 percent.
The stock market immediately rallied, with the FTSE 100 index of leading stocks hitting a record high of just over 5,063.4 points, up over 0.7 percent on the day.
Buyers were also active on the government bond market, with the key September Gilts contract rising 12/32 to 115-01 just after the Bank of England announcement.
Ciaran Barr, an economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said it was important to note that the Bank of England thought rates were now high enough to keep inflation in check.
"That is a clear signal that the Bank thinks it has done enough for the time being and it believes the move should put pressure on sterling," Barr said.
Barr said no further rate rise was now expected until November.
Sterling dropped just over one pfennig after the interest rate rise, falling to 3.0020/30 marks from 3.0130/40 before the news.
The pound has risen by over 20 percent in the last year, driving down profits at large British exporters.

The Bank of England agreed that the pound was putting "severe pressure" on businesses exposed to international competition, but said its strength mainly reflected factors outside of the Bank's own control.

Some economists thought the Bank of England might not be expecting any major weakening in the pound and its hopes of keeping inflation under control were linked to a view that sterling will remain firm.
Andrew Milligan, an analyst with General Accident, also believed that interest rates were now high enough to keep inflation in check.
But he added, "This will be on the basis that sterling remains at current levels or even appreciates further."
The Bank of England might have to raise rates again if the pound started to depreciate, Milligan said.
